characterized_levers.name: Technical Feasibility Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Demonstrating technical feasibility impacts policy. Immediate: Demonstrators built → Systemic: 15% increased policy traction due to concrete evidence → Strategic: Enhanced credibility in procurement negotiations.
options: Focus demonstrator efforts on a single, highly secure authentication method, such as FIDO2, on a mainstream Android device.
Develop demonstrators for both FIDO2 on GrapheneOS and a browser-based fallback, accepting slightly longer development timelines.
Explore passwordless authentication via blockchain-anchored identity and decentralized identifiers (DIDs) alongside FIDO2 and browser-based fallback demonstrators.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Technical Risk vs. Scope. Weakness: The options don't explicitly address the cost implications of each demonstrator approach.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on demonstrating technical feasibility to impact policy, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of the technical demonstrators on policy traction, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to demonstrator development.
characterized_levers.description: This lever controls the technical strategy for building non-production demonstrators that prove platform-neutral and fallback-capable authentication is feasible without exclusive reliance on Apple or Google. It shapes the scope, timeline, and credibility of technical evidence produced in phases two and three. Success is measured by delivering working demonstrators that exemplify standards-based approaches (FIDO2/WebAuthn, OpenID Connect) on privacy-respecting platforms or browser-based fallback paths, generating concrete proof-of-concept that informs procurement language and standards pressure rather than attempting production integration.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Technical Feasibility Strategy amplifies Policy Advocacy Strategy by providing empirical evidence that strengthens policy proposals and makes procurement neutrality harder to dismiss as unrealistic. It also enables Procurement Influence Strategy by delivering tangible demonstrators that can be cited in official design and procurement documents, directly supporting the evidence base for platform-neutral requirements in AltID and related systems.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Broader demonstrator scope (blockchain-anchored DIDs alongside FIDO2 and browser-based paths) extends timelines and costs, potentially delaying Coalition Building Strategy's stakeholder engagement momentum and weakening Phase one's ability to secure early institutional commitment. Conversely, narrow focus on a single method reduces policy and procurement leverage, limiting the breadth of evidence supporting EU Standards Engagement Strategy's push for diversified, interoperable approaches.

characterized_levers.name: Policy Advocacy Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Policy advocacy shapes procurement. Immediate: Policy proposals submitted → Systemic: 20% greater likelihood of influencing AltID requirements → Strategic: Increased adoption of platform-neutral standards.
options: Focus advocacy on continuity of service and supplier concentration risks, avoiding direct privacy arguments.
Balance continuity arguments with privacy and democratic accountability concerns, broadening the coalition.
Prioritize open-source governance and community-led development models for digital identity, framing platform neutrality as a public good.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Political Risk vs. Coalition Size. Weakness: The options don't consider the potential for regulatory capture by incumbent vendors.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on policy advocacy shaping procurement, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of policy advocacy on influencing AltID requirements, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to advocacy focus.
characterized_levers.description: This lever shapes the framing, messaging, and institutional targets of advocacy efforts across all phases. It determines whether arguments emphasize resilience and supplier concentration risk, expand to include privacy and democratic accountability, or prioritize open-source governance models. It directly influences which stakeholders join the coalition, how sympathetic policymakers and officials perceive the problem, and whether procurement or standards bodies view platform neutrality as a legitimate priority rather than ideological preference.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Policy Advocacy Strategy directly enables Coalition Building Strategy by framing the issue in terms that resonate across diverse stakeholders—security experts, civil-society organisations, privacy advocates, and procurement officials all respond more readily to continuity and resilience arguments than to abstract ideological claims. Balanced framing also strengthens Procurement Influence Strategy by making platform-neutral requirements appear pragmatic rather than activist.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Prioritizing open-source governance and community-led models may alienate pragmatic procurement and government officials who prioritize operational continuity and vendor accountability, weakening Procurement Influence Strategy's traction. Conversely, narrowing advocacy to only continuity risks excludes privacy advocates and democratic-accountability constituencies, constraining Coalition Building Strategy's breadth and reducing political protection against incumbent vendor pushback.

characterized_levers.name: Coalition Building Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Coalition strength amplifies advocacy. Immediate: Stakeholder engagement increased → Systemic: 30% stronger advocacy position in procurement discussions → Strategic: Greater political pressure for platform neutrality.
options: Build a narrow coalition focused on security experts and contingency-planning stakeholders.
Expand the coalition to include civil-society organizations, privacy advocates, and academic researchers.
Actively recruit dissenting voices from within the MitID operator and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen to foster internal debate.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Speed vs. Breadth of Support. Weakness: The options fail to address the potential for conflicting priorities within the coalition.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on coalition building to amplify advocacy, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of coalition strength on advocacy position, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to coalition composition.
characterized_levers.description: Coalition Building Strategy mobilizes diverse stakeholder groups—civil-society organizations, privacy advocates, academic researchers, security experts, contingency-planning stakeholders, and sympathetic political actors—to amplify advocacy reach and credibility. Success depends on securing organizational commitments, establishing shared messaging frameworks, and maintaining alignment across divergent priorities. Key metrics include coalition size, institutional representation breadth, public statements of support, and demonstrated ability to coordinate joint advocacy activities during critical procurement and policy windows.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: This lever strongly amplifies Policy Advocacy Strategy and Procurement Influence Strategy. A cohesive coalition provides credible external pressure on Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and procurement decision-makers, making advocacy messaging harder to dismiss as isolated activism. Coalition visibility also strengthens EU Standards Engagement Strategy by demonstrating pan-European stakeholder concern about platform dependency, elevating the profile of platform-neutrality arguments in broader identity wallet discussions.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Coalition-building creates tension with Technical Feasibility Strategy's lean, focused scope. Broader coalitions demand tangible technical outputs earlier to sustain engagement, potentially pressuring demonstrator work beyond defensible lean prototyping. Additionally, recruiting dissenting internal voices from MitID operators risks fragmenting coalition coherence if institutional stakeholders' concerns diverge fundamentally from civil-society demands around sovereignty versus pragmatic interoperability.

characterized_levers.name: Procurement Influence Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Procurement influence drives adoption. Immediate: Platform-neutral language included in procurement documents → Systemic: 25% faster scaling through mandated supplier diversity → Strategic: Reduced long-term dependency on Apple and Google.
options: Focus on including general language about supplier concentration risk in AltID procurement documents.
Advocate for specific requirements for platform-neutral access and certified fallback authentication paths.
Propose a 'digital sovereignty bonus' in procurement scoring, rewarding vendors who demonstrably reduce platform dependency.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Specificity vs. Implementability. Weakness: The options don't account for the potential for vendors to game the procurement process.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on procurement influence driving adoption, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of procurement influence on scaling, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to procurement language.
characterized_levers.description: Procurement Influence Strategy shapes AltID and related digital identity procurement documents to embed platform-neutrality, fallback-access, and supplier-concentration language at the specification and scoring stage. Success requires credible technical evidence, coalition pressure, and direct stakeholder engagement with procurement authorities. Key metrics include adoption of platform-neutral language in official procurement documents, inclusion of fallback-authentication requirements, scoring adjustments favoring vendor diversity, and documented acknowledgment by Digitaliseringsstyrelsen or procuring bodies that supplier concentration constitutes a material risk.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: This lever directly depends on both Technical Feasibility Strategy and Coalition Building Strategy. Demonstrators provide proof-of-concept evidence that platform-neutral access is technically achievable, making procurement language defensible. Coalition visibility applies external political pressure simultaneously, making procurement offices more receptive to supplier-neutrality requirements. Together, these levers create a pincer movement: technical credibility from below, stakeholder pressure from outside, making resistance costlier for procurement decision-makers.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Procurement Influence Strategy risks direct conflict with EU Standards Engagement Strategy if divergent requirements emerge between Danish procurement specifications and evolving European Digital Identity Wallet frameworks. Overly specific Danish requirements could isolate rather than align with EU harmonization efforts. Additionally, aggressive procurement language demanding platform-neutral access may provoke vendor pushback and delay adoption, potentially contradicting the project's goal of influencing AltID before the identity stack hardens further.

characterized_levers.name: EU Standards Engagement Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: EU standards engagement creates broader impact. Immediate: Input provided to relevant EU bodies → Systemic: 10% increased alignment with European Digital Identity Wallet requirements → Strategic: Enhanced interoperability and reduced lock-in across Europe.
options: Monitor relevant EU bodies and technical working groups, providing occasional input on interoperability.
Actively engage with EU bodies, advocating for platform-neutral access and certified fallback mechanisms in eIDAS2 and related standards.
Champion a 'sovereign identity sandbox' within the EU Digital Identity Wallet framework to test and validate platform-neutral authentication models.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Resource Allocation vs. Scope of Influence. Weakness: The options don't address the potential for EU standards to be influenced by large platform vendors.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on EU standards engagement creating broader impact, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of EU standards engagement on alignment with European Digital Identity Wallet requirements, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to EU engagement strategies.
characterized_levers.description: EU Standards Engagement Strategy directs the project's involvement with European Digital Identity Wallet framework and related EU technical working groups. It controls the intensity and scope of advocacy for platform-neutral access requirements, certified fallback mechanisms, and interoperability standards at the EU level. Success is measured by inclusion of supplier-concentration and resilience language in official EU digital identity materials, alignment with broader European requirements, and contribution to standards that reduce lock-in across member states. This lever amplifies the project's impact beyond Denmark, creating precedent and structural support for domestic policy wins.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: EU Standards Engagement Strategy strongly synergizes with Policy Advocacy Strategy, as EU-level standards language provides regulatory leverage for Danish procurement and policy arguments. It also amplifies Procurement Influence Strategy by establishing international normative pressure that makes supplier-neutral requirements harder for AltID and related programs to resist. EU standards adoption creates a institutional backdrop that legitimizes domestic fallback-access mandates.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: EU Standards Engagement Strategy conflicts with Technical Feasibility Strategy and Coalition Building Strategy through resource and attention constraints. Engaging EU bodies during phase three competes for limited project capacity with finalizing demonstrators and consolidating domestic stakeholder support. Additionally, large platform vendors already have established influence channels in EU standard-setting bodies, potentially marginalizing the project's input unless strategic partners and published evidence are leveraged simultaneously.
